links.outcome: Genki specificity versus 10 human readers at matched sensitivity for TB screening
links.effect: At matched sensitivity (79.0%), Genki specificity was 95.2% (DICOM) and 92.1% (JPEG) versus 84.8% for human readers, p < 0.001.
links.quote: The corresponding specificity for the Genki software is significantly higher than the human readers, whether using the DICOM (84.8% vs 95.2%, p < 0.001) or JPEG files (84.8% vs 92.1%, p < 0.001).

links.outcome: AUC and specificity when input format changes from DICOM to photographed film JPEG
links.effect: AUC did not differ significantly (0.94 vs 0.92, p = 0.190), but specificity was significantly lower with JPEG (e.g., 95.2% vs 92.1%, p < 0.001) and abnormality scores were higher.
links.quote: There is no significant difference in the AUC for the Genki CAD software when processing either DICOM or JPEG files (0.94 vs 0.92, p = 0.190).

links.outcome: Performance variation by acquisition format (DICOM vs photographed film); no site-specific analysis
links.effect: AUC was similar across file types, but specificity was significantly lower with JPEG at matched thresholds (81.1% vs 89.3% at 91.4% sensitivity, p < 0.001).
links.quote: Although the Genki CAD software met the TPP criteria when using photographs of printed X-ray films, its specificity was significantly lower compared to processing DICOM files.

links.outcome: Specificity after choosing tuned abnormality score thresholds to reach target sensitivity
links.effect: Calibrating thresholds to 90% sensitivity gave specificity of 89.3% (DICOM) and 81.1% (JPEG), meeting the TPP criteria.
links.quote: When the software's abnormality score thresholds were calibrated to achieve 90% sensitivity, Genki maintained high specificity with both DICOM (89.3%) and JPEG (81.1%) file types, meeting the minimum Target Product Profile (TPP) criteria for a high-sensitivity, high-specificity screening test.
